summary: TechCrunch's Harri Weber reviews small and affordable EVs and e-mobility companies that failed, were cancelled or retreated in 2023, arguing the market is dominated by large, costly vehicles because "big sells." Casualties include the ElectraMeccanica Solo, Honda e, Sono Sion, the GM-Honda affordable EV partnership, the US Mazda MX-30, Revel mopeds and VanMoof. The piece closes with bright spots such as booming bike-share programs, the Fiat 500e's North American arrival and startup Telo Trucks.
one_line: A roundup of small, affordable EVs and e-mobility ventures that flopped or were cancelled in 2023, plus a few remaining bright spots.
key_facts: ElectraMeccanica's Solo was legally a motorcycle, a three-wheeled one-seater with 100 miles of range and an $18,500 price tag; the company recalled every Solo in April 2023 over power failure issues.
ElectraMeccanica planned to merge with electric truck maker Tevva but pulled the plug on that deal in October.
The Honda e debuted in Europe and Japan in 2020 with a 100-mile range and a $36,000-$43,000 price tag, and Honda said it would cease production in January 2024 after poor sales.

German automaker Sono priced the five-seater solar Sono Sion at $25,000 and planned to start production in 2023, but instead pivoted to selling solar tech to third-party automakers and laid off 300 workers.

General Motors and Honda announced in April 2022 that they would co-develop millions of small EVs under $30,000 for North America, targeting 2027, but canceled the collaboration in October 2023 citing "extensive studies and analysis."

Mazda sold the MX-30 in the U.S. only in California and said in July 2023 it would discontinue it in the U.S. at the end of 2023, while continuing sales in Japan and the EU; the MX-30 has a 100-mile range.
Revel's moped ridership peaked in July 2020 at nearly 600,000 rides in a month, then collapsed amid several deaths involving Revel mopeds; the company dropped mopeds in favor of electric cars.
VanMoof raised a $128 million Series C and billed itself the "most funded e-bike company in the world," but lost money on each bike due to costly repairs tied to proprietary parts.

VanMoof paused sales and co-founder Taco Carlier left as the company declared bankruptcy in summer 2023; Lavoie acquired it in August for "tens of millions" but had not restarted production or repairs months later.
D.C.'s Capitol Bikeshare recorded a record 428,000 rides in May, and New York's Citi Bike recorded 867,838 rides in a single week that month.
The Fiat 500e is coming to North America in 2024 in limited quantities, and Arcimoto remains a three-wheeled EV holdout in the U.S.
Telo Trucks is developing a pickup with the footprint of a two-door Mini Cooper, and GM now says it will keep the Chevy Bolt EUV after saying it would kill the Bolt lineup.
